'''trona''' (trō′nä), ''n.'' [Prob. a North African form ult. connected with ''natron''.] The native soda of Egypt, a hydrous carbonate of sodium, Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>.HNaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O. {{smaller|It also occurs at Borax Lake, San Bernardino county, California, in Churchill county, Nevada, and elsewhere. '''tronage''' (tron′āj), ''n.'' [< ''tron'' + ''-age''.] 1. A royal tax upon wool. See ''tronator''.—2. See the quotation.

{{smaller block|Next unto this stockes is the parish church of S. Mary Woll-Church, so called of a beame placed in the church-yard which was thereof called Wooll church-haw, of the ''tronage'', or weighing of wooll there used.

'''tronator''' (tron′ā-tor), ''n.'' [ML., < ''trona'', a tron: see ''tron'', ''trone''<sup>1</sup>.] An official whose duty it was to weigh wool and receive the custom or toll termed ''tronage''. ''Archæol. Inst. Jour.'', XVII. 165.

Hence—4. The command by commission and rank of such a troop of horse.

{{smaller block|His papa would have purchased him a ''troop''—nay, a lieutenant-colonelcy—some day, but for his fatal excesses.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Fitz Boodle's Confessions.}}}}

5. A band or company of performers; a troupe.—6. A particular roll or call of the drum; a signal for marching.

{{smaller block|Tony's beat of the ''troop'' was the signal for the soldiers to assemble.
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 13.}}}}

7. A herd or flock of beasts or birds: as, a ''troop'' of antelopes or sparrows.—'''Household troops.''' {{smaller|See ''household''.}}—'''Subsidiary troops.''' {{smaller|See ''subsidiary''.}}

'''troop''' (tröp), ''v.'' [< ''troop'', ''n.''] I. ''intrans.'' 1. To assemble or gather in crowds; flock together.

{{smaller block|What would ye, soldiers? wherefore ''troop'' ye
Like mutinous madmen thus?
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, iv. 7.}}
Now from the roost . . .
Come ''trooping'' at the housewife's well-known call
The feather'd tribes domestic. ''Cowper'', Task, v. 61.
The Maids of Nazareth, as they ''trooped'' to fill
Their balanced urns beside the mountain rill.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', The Mother's Secret.}}}}

2. To march; to march in or form part of a troop or company.

{{smaller block|Nor do I as an enemy to peace
''Troop'' in the throngs of military men.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 1. 62.}}}}

3. To march off in haste.

{{smaller block|Aurora's harbinger,
At whose approach, ghosts, wandering here and there,
''Troop'' home to churchyards. ''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 2. 382.}}

[< ''trollop'' + ''-ing''2.] Slovenly; sluttish; trollopish. {{smaller block|"Saw ever ony body the like o' that?" "Yes, you abominable woman," vociferated the traveller, "many have seen the like of it, and all will see the like of it that have anything to do with your ''trolloping'' sex!" {{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, i.}}}} '''trollopish''' (trol′ọp-ish), ''a.'' [< ''trollop'' + ''-ish''1.] Like a trollop, especially in the sense of loosely or carelessly dressed, or accustomed to dress carelessly and without neatness; slovenly and loose in habit: noting a woman. '''trollopy''' (trol′ọp-i), ''a.'' [< ''trollop'' + ''-y''1.] Same as ''trollopish. Jane Austen'', Mansfield Park, xxxviii. '''troll-plate''' (trōl′plāt), ''n.'' In ''mach.'', a rotating disk employed to effect the simultaneous convergence or divergence of a number of objects, such as screw-dies in a stock, or the jaws of a universal chuck. ''E. H. Knight.'' '''trolly,''' ''n.'' See ''trolley.'' '''tromba''' (trom′bä), ''n.'' [It.: see ''trump''1.] Same as ''trumpet.''—'''Tromba marina.''' {{smaller|Same as ''sea-trumpet'', 1.}} '''trombidiid''' (trom-bid′i-id), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' (Leach, 1814, as ''Trombidides''), < ''Trombidium'' + ''-idæ.''] A family of tracheate acarids, whose type genus is ''Trombidium;'' the ground-, gar- ''trommel'', according as it is used for sizing or for cleaning ores. See ''sizing''1, 3. {{smaller block|A ''trommel'' is a barrel in the form of a cylinder or of a truncated cone, horizontal or slightly inclined, turning round its own axis. It is the machine employed for similar purposes in most other industries; the only wonder is that so long a time elapsed before it was adopted in dressing ores, for it furnishes the best possible means not only of cleaning the ore, but also of sizing it. {{right|''Callon'', Lectures on Mining (trans.).}}}} '''tromometer''' (trọ̄-mom′e-tėr), ''n.'' [< Gr. τρόμος, a trembling (< τρέμειν = L. [< ''tromometer'' + ''-ic.''] Of or pertaining to the tromometer. ''Nature'', XLIII. 520. '''trompe†, trompe1†.''' Obsolete forms of ''trump''1. '''trompe2''' (tromp), ''n.'' [F. ''trompe'', lit. a trump: see ''trump''1.] The apparatus by which the blast is produced in the Catalan forge. {{smaller|It is a simple, effective, and ingenious contrivance for producing a continuous and equable blast, but its use is restricted to localities where a fall of water from a height of several yards can be obtained. The principle is that water can be made to fall through a pipe in such a way that it will draw in through side openings a considerable amount of air, which by a simple and ingenious arrangement can be utilized as a constant current or blast, and which has the merit of costing almost nothing. It has been utilized to a limited extent elsewhere than in the department of Ari ge, in the south of France, where it was formerly very}} den-, harvest-, or soldier-mites, which have the palpi converted into raptorial organs. {{smaller|They are closely related to the ''Tetranychidæ'', or spinning-mites, but are larger, velvety and opaque, and usually of brilliant colors, as scarlet or vermilion. They also differ in being predaceous and carnivorous, the spinning-mites being vegetable-feeders. Several genera and many species have been described, and the family is represented in all parts of the world. ''Trombidium fasciculatum'' of the East Indies, one third of an inch long, is the largest acarid known. The ''Trombidiidæ'' are strictly predatory in the adult stage, but their larvæ, although originally no more parasitic than a gnat or a leech, will yet attach themselves to the bodies of animals, or even to man himself, and are usually separated only by death or artificial means, causing considerable irritation while present. Some are known by the name of ''harvest-bug'' in England, and ''rouget'' in France, being the ''Leptus autumnalis'' of earlier entomologists.}} {{smaller block|generally employed.
